headline.funnel_interpretation: Egger’s test is generally not recommended when fewer than 10 studies are available.
headline.results_interpretation: The pooled analysis of 2 studies yielded an effect size of 1.38 (95% CI: 0.83–2.32), indicating no statistically significant association between monounsaturated fat (mufa) and renal cell carcinoma. Although the point estimate suggests a potential positive relationship, the confidence interval includes the null. These findings were accompanied by very high heterogeneity (I² = 80.19%), reflecting highly inconsistent results across studies.

cases.excerpt: A total of 1478 incident cases of renal cell cancer were identified (709 in women and 769 in men).

effect_size.excerpt: By comparison, the pooled multivariable RR for the highest vs the lowest quintile of total fat intake was 1.10 (95% CI = 0.92 to 1.32; P trend = .31) and of total protein intake was 1.06 (95% CI = 0.89 to 1.26; P trend = .37). Intakes of red meat, processed meat, poultry, or seafood were not associated with the risk of renal cell cancer.

sample_size.excerpt: For 323 cases and 1820 controls from the present study, information on dietary intake from foods high in fat nutrients and other lifestyle factors was obtained using a mailed questionnaire.
sample_size.location: abstract; total_n derived from reported group counts 323 + 1820 = 2143

cases.excerpt: For 323 cases and 1820 controls from the present study, information on dietary intake from foods high in fat nutrients and other lifestyle factors was obtained using a mailed questionnaire.

effect_size.excerpt: Dietary nutrient intake of animal fat, saturated fat, oleic acid and cholesterol was associated with an elevated risk of RCC (OR = 1.9, 95 % CI 1.3, 2.9, P trend < 0.001; OR = 2.6, 95 % CI 1.6, 4.0, P trend < 0.001; OR = 1.9, 95 % CI 1.2, 2.9, P trend = 0.01; OR = 1.9, 95 % CI 1.3, 2.8, P trend = 0.006, respectively, for the top quartile compared with the bottom quartile of intake).

confidence_interval.excerpt: Dietary nutrient intake of animal fat, saturated fat, oleic acid and cholesterol was associated with an elevated risk of RCC (OR = 1.9, 95 % CI 1.3, 2.9, P trend < 0.001; OR = 2.6, 95 % CI 1.6, 4.0, P trend < 0.001; OR = 1.9, 95 % CI 1.2, 2.9, P trend = 0.01; OR = 1.9, 95 % CI 1.3, 2.8, P trend = 0.006, respectively, for the top quartile compared with the bottom quartile of intake).
